questions.question: What does a “reproducible build” mean in the strictest sense?
options: Given the same inputs, independent builds produce identical bytes (the same artifact hash)
The build completes without errors on at least one machine
The code compiles quickly and uses few dependencies
The artifact is signed, so it must be safe to run
questions.explanation: Reproducibility is about determinism: the same inputs yield the same output bytes, so hashes are comparable.

questions.question: What does a signed release primarily give you (assuming you already trust the public key)?
options: Authenticity and integrity of a specific digest/statement about the release
A guarantee that the build is free of vulnerabilities
A guarantee that dependencies are automatically pinned
A guarantee that the artifact is encrypted end-to-end
questions.explanation: Signatures let you verify that a specific hash/manifest came from the expected signing identity and was not modified.

questions.question: Which of these is a common cause of non-reproducible archives even when file contents are identical?
options: Timestamps and metadata embedded into archive entries or compression headers
Using SHA-256 instead of SHA-1 for hashing
Using hex encoding for hashes instead of base64
Using JSON instead of YAML for the manifest
questions.explanation: Archive formats often store mtimes, uid/gid, and file order; if you don’t fix them, identical inputs can produce different bytes.

questions.question: Why is a build manifest useful even if you also publish an artifact hash?
options: It makes the build contents explicit by listing each file and its hash, so you can detect missing/extra files
It replaces the need for any cryptographic hash function
It guarantees the artifact is encrypted at rest
It ensures all dependencies are automatically verified by pip
questions.explanation: A manifest turns “this is the hash” into “these are the exact files and bytes that make up the release”.

questions.question: What is the most important boundary to cover with a signature in a basic release verification flow?
options: A digest derived from the exact build contents (e.g., the manifest tree hash)
Only the version string (e.g., “v1.2.3”) so users know what they downloaded
Only the release filename so mirrors can rename it safely
Only the README so users can trust the documentation
questions.explanation: Signing a content-derived digest binds the signature to the actual bytes that matter, not just labels.

questions.question: Attack scenario: a mirror is compromised and replaces the release tarball. What stops this in a signed-release flow?
options: Users verify the signature using a pinned/trusted public key and reject artifacts whose digest doesn’t match the signed statement
Users install from the mirror faster so the attacker has less time
Users only download over HTTPS, which makes tampering impossible
Users compress the tarball again locally to “normalize” it
questions.explanation: A compromised mirror can serve anything; signatures work because the attacker can’t forge the signer’s key.

questions.question: Which public-key distribution method is the most fragile if it’s your only trust anchor?
options: Downloading the public key from the same unsigned, unverified channel as the artifact
Pinning the public key in multiple independent locations (repo + website + transparency log)
Out-of-band key fingerprint verification (e.g., in-person or via a trusted directory)
Using a transparency log so key changes are publicly visible
questions.explanation: If the attacker can swap both the artifact and the key in the same channel, verification becomes meaningless.

questions.question: When verifying a release against a manifest, what should the verifier reject?
options: Artifacts that contain extra files not listed in the manifest (or omit files that are listed)
Artifacts that use a different filename than expected
Artifacts that are larger than 10MB
Artifacts whose README contains a different title
questions.explanation: A manifest is only meaningful if it fully describes the artifact contents; extra or missing files are a red flag.
